title: Prepare horses and clients for a trail ride of up to one day

lessons.title: Preparing the horses and equipment
lessons.html:
Matching horses to the ride

Trail rides through the veld, mountains, beaches or vineyards are popular with tourists and locals. A safe ride starts the day before, with horses that are fit, sound and suitable for the route and for clients of different abilities.

Checking each horse

  1. Health: eating and drinking normally, normal temperature, no coughing or nasal discharge.
  2. Soundness: trot up on firm ground; no lameness or heat in the legs.
  3. Feet: shoes secure or bare feet in good condition for the terrain; pick out hooves.
  4. Back and girth area: no sores, swelling or sensitivity.
  5. Fitness: suited to the distance and climbs. Rest horses that worked hard the day before.
  6. Temperament: the quietest, most reliable horses for beginners and children.

Tack

  • Saddles that fit both horse and rider, with clean numnahs.
  • Check girths, stirrup leathers, buckles and stitching. Replace worn items.
  • Bridles fitted correctly with suitable bits. A headcollar under the bridle and a lead rope tied to the saddle are useful on trails.
  • Saddle bags for the guide: first aid kits for horse and rider, hoof pick, knife, spare lead rope, a cell phone or radio, water.

Planning the route

  • Know the route, distance, terrain, water points, gates and hazards such as dongas, bogs, steep slopes, roads, fences and livestock.
  • Check the weather forecast: heat, storms and lightning are serious risks in summer.
  • Get permission to ride on neighbouring land and close every gate as you found it.
  • Tell someone at the base the route and expected return time.

lessons.title: Preparing and briefing clients
lessons.html:
Assessing clients

Before the ride, ask each client about:

  • Riding experience: never ridden, beginner, intermediate or experienced.
  • Weight and height, to match a suitable horse; many yards have a weight limit.
  • Medical conditions, allergies (e.g. bee stings), pregnancy and medication.
  • Emergency contact details.

Clients sign an indemnity form, which explains the risks of riding. Read it with them if needed. An indemnity form does not remove your duty of care.

Clothing and equipment for clients

  • An approved riding helmet, correctly fitted and fastened. Compulsory.
  • Closed shoes with a small heel; no sandals or bare feet.
  • Long trousers to prevent chafing.
  • Sunscreen, hat for breaks, sunglasses with a strap, water bottle.
  • No loose scarves or dangling bags.

The safety briefing

  1. Introduce the guides and the horses by name.
  2. Demonstrate how to mount and dismount safely and how to hold the reins.
  3. Explain how to stop, steer and slow down.
  4. Rules: stay in single file, one horse length apart; do not overtake the lead guide; do not let horses eat grass on the trail; tell a guide if you feel uncomfortable.
  5. What to do if a horse spooks: sit deep, heels down, hold the reins and the saddle, and call to the guide.
  6. Explain the route, duration, stops and the speed of the ride (walk only, or some trotting for those able).

Mounting and final check

Help clients mount from a block; adjust stirrups and tighten girths. Watch each client walk in the arena or yard before leaving. If someone cannot control their horse, give them a quieter horse or a lead rein.

Key points

  • Check each horse's health, soundness, feet, back and fitness.
  • Inspect all tack and pack first aid and communication kits.
  • Plan the route, check weather and tell base your plans.
  • Assess clients' experience and health and match horses carefully.
  • Helmets and closed shoes are compulsory; give a clear safety briefing.
